# Introduction

## Background: Cardiomyopathy

Cardiomyopathy is a group of diseases that affect the heart muscle, leading to structural and functional abnormalities that impair the heart’s ability to pump blood efficiently. These conditions can result in serious clinical outcomes, including heart failure, arrhythmias, and sudden cardiac death.

Many forms of cardiomyopathy have a genetic basis. Inherited mutations have been associated with several types of the disease, such as hypertrophic, dilated, restrictive, and arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy, as well as left ventricular non-compaction and ion channelopathies. These mutations often affect genes involved in heart muscle structure and function, including those related to the sarcomere, cytoskeleton, and ion channels.

## Aim and Research Questions

The aim of this project is to identify and evaluate genetic variants associated with cardiomyopathy using DNA sequencing data. By comparing the patient’s DNA sequence to established cardiomyopathy-associated gene panels, potentially pathogenic variants can be detected and assessed. Using next-generation sequencing (NGS) technologies, this project seeks to identify genetic variants that may contribute to the development and progression of cardiomyopathy and to evaluate their relevance in a diagnostic context.

## Tools

|  Tool   |              Purpose              |
|:-------:|:---------------------------------:|
| RStudio |        Reporting framework        |
| Galaxy  |     Data processing pipeline      |
| GitHub  | Version control and collaboration |

## Analysis Workflow

The overall analysis workflow is designed to identify and characterize genetic variants from DNA sequencing data. The workflow includes quality control of raw reads, read preprocessing, alignment to a reference genome, variant calling, variant filtering and annotation.

# Data and Quality Control

## Data

The dataset used in this project consists of DNA sequencing data obtained from patients diagnosed with cardiomyopathy. The data were provided as part of a master-level genomics course and were used for educational and research purposes.

### Number of Samples

The dataset consists of multiple patient samples derived from cardiomyopathy cases. In this project, the analysis focuses on **Sample 1**, which is provided as paired-end sequencing data consisting of two read files (forward and reverse reads).

### File Format

The sequencing data were provided in FASTQ format, containing the raw reads generated by next-generation sequencing and used as the input for the analysis. This is the first line in the file:

```         
@M01234:01:000000000-A1B2C:1:1101:16810:1655 2:N:0:2
AATGACATTGATCTCCACAGCCATCAAGAGCCCATTCAAGATGACCATCATGCCTGTGATGCAGAAACGCAGGTTTGATATGTCCAAGCCAGACTGACAGTACTTAACCAATTTTATTGTTTTTGTAATAAAGGCCCTTACCCAATACAGG
+
11A11DDFDDB@GGGGCF11FA1GGF1GBCCBFHHHHGHFCGHFFHFHB1F1FFHBF1BG2DFBGF1FC/EE/A1D/1A2DBGGHFFFE/000FG11BF1GFGFHHFHHEHHHGHHGBDFHFHG/BE2F2>FH1>E/FE11BG</B1<110
```

Each line describes the following:

-   An identifier for the sequencing machine, the chip it used and the specific position within it.
-   The DNA nucleotides in order given by the sequence.
-   A plus sign.
-   A corresponding quality identifier for each nucleotide, also given by the sequencer.

## Quality Control

Quality control of raw sequencing reads was performed to evaluate data quality before downstream analysis. For this purpose, the tool **Falco** was used. A `.fastQ.gz` file was provided as input, and Falco generates several plots as output. Each plot highlights a specific aspect of the sequencing data, such as base quality scores, GC content, sequence length distribution, and the presence of adapter contamination, and provides a quality assessment in the form of [pass]{style="color:#009900"}, [warn]{style="color:#999900"} or [fail]{style="color:#990000"}.

```{=html}
<pre style="background-color:#dee2e6; color:#2c3143; border:none">
<b>Falco</b> An alternative, more performant implementation of FastQC for high throughput sequence quality control
(Galaxy Version 1.2.4+galaxy0)
</pre>
```

This is because no value is below 10 and no median is below 25. Quality decreases at the end of the sequences due to [phasing](https://www.ecseq.com/support/ngs/why-does-the-sequence-quality-decrease-over-the-read-in-illumina). This is a small chance that a nucleotide is misplaced, which with longer sequences adds up. |
| **Per tile sequence quality** examines quality variation between different tiles on the flow cell using a color scale where blue indicates average or above-average quality and red indicates lower quality. A warning is issued if any tile falls more than **2** Phred scores below the mean, and failure if more than **5** below. Our results show consistent blue coloration across all tiles with no significant deviations, confirming that the data **passes** this quality control check. ![](./assets/quality_res_byROA/Per%20tile%20sequence%20quality1.png) | This test gives quality scores on each base pair position per tile in the sequencer flow cell. A heat map like pattern represents above average values with cold colors and below average values with hot ones. ![](./assets/quality-test/r2/per-tile-sequence-quality.png) The test resulted in a pass and there are no consistent low values for any given tile. |
| **Per sequence quality scores** examine whether subsets of sequences have universally low quality values, which may indicate systematic issues like poor imaging at flow cell edges. A warning is issued if the most frequently observed mean quality falls below **27 (0.2% error rate)**, and failure occurs below **20 (1% error rate)**. In our results, the majority of sequences have mean quality scores above 30, well above both thresholds, confirming that the data passes this quality check. ![](./assets/quality_res_byROA/Per%20sequence%20quality%20scores1.png) | This plot shows the amount of sequences per Phred score, the highest density value being the average score. ![](./assets/quality-test/r2/per-sequence-quality-scores.png) This test resulted in a pass as the most frequently observed values are above 27. |
| **Per base sequence content** analyzes the proportion of each nucleotide (A, T, C, G) at every position across all reads. In a properly balanced library, the lines for each base should run parallel with only small differences between A and T or G and C. A warning is issued if the difference between A and T or G and C exceeds **10%** at any position, and failure occurs if the difference exceeds **20%**. ![](./assets/quality_res_byROA/Per%20base%20sequence%20content1.png) In our results, the data failed this module. As shown, there is a consistent imbalance between A and T across most positions, with A averaging around **29%** while T averages only **21%**, creating a difference of approximately **8%**. While this difference is below the failure threshold, it still exceeds the warning threshold, indicating a systematic bias in nucleotide distribution that may need to be addressed before further analysis. | Here the percentage amount of each nucleotide A, C, T and G is plotted per base pair position. It is expected to have a equally consistent amount of A and T as well as C and G. ![](./assets/quality-test/r2/per-base-sequence-content.png) This test resulted in a fail. However, all sequencers produce inaccurate readings for this test at the start of the sequence. |
| **Per sequence GC content** measures the distribution of G and C bases across all reads, plotted as the number of reads versus GC percentage. A normal distribution is expected for high-quality data, with the peak matching the genome's overall GC content. ![](./assets/quality_res_byROA/Per%20sequence%20GC%20content1.png) Our results passed this module, showing a GC distribution that closely follows the theoretical distribution. As shown, the highest density of reads occurs at **50-60%** GC, which aligns well with the expected pattern for this dataset. This indicates no significant GC bias in the sequencing data. | This plot shows the Guanine and Cytosine percent amount against a theoretical normal distribution. ![](./assets/quality-test/r2/per-sequence-gc-content.png) The result is a pass given that the sum of deviation from the normal distribution does not exceed 15% of all reads. |
| **Per base N content** measures the proportion of ambiguous base calls (N) at each position across all reads. Low N content, especially near read ends, is normal and expected. A warning is issued if any position exceeds **5%** N content, and failure occurs if above **20%**. Our results passed this module, with N content remaining consistently low **(below 0.04%)** across all positions. This indicates high-quality base calling with minimal ambiguity throughout the sequencing run. ![](./assets/quality_res_byROA/Per%20base%20N%20content1.png) | If the sequencer is unable to confidently assign a base it will substitute it with an N. This test shows the percent amount of N per base pair position. ![](./assets/quality-test/r2/per-base-n-content.png) The test resulted in a pass, because no position has more than 5%. |
| **Sequence length distribution** analyzes the range of fragment sizes in the raw sequencing data. A warning is issued if all sequences are not the same length, while failure occurs if any sequence has zero length. Our results show a warning in this module, indicating that the reads in our raw dataset are not all identical in length. ![](./assets/quality_res_byROA/Sequence%20Length%20Distribution1.png) | ![](./assets/quality-test/r2/sequence-length-distribution.png) |
| **Sequence duplication levels** measure the proportion of duplicate reads in the sequencing data. This module identifies reads that appear more than once, which can indicate over-amplification during library preparation. A warning is issued when non-unique reads make up more than **20%** of the total sequences. Our results show a warning in this module, indicating a moderate level of duplication in the dataset. ![](./assets/quality_res_byROA/Sequence%20Duplication%20Levels1.png) | ![](./assets/quality-test/r2/sequence-duplication-levels.png) |
| **Overrepresented sequences** are those that appear more frequently than expected in the dataset. Our results passed this module as no overrepresented sequences were found. |  |
| **Adapter content** assesses the presence of adapter sequences in the reads, which can occur when fragments are shorter than the read length. A warning is issued if any adapter is present in more than **5%** of reads, and failure occurs if above **10%**. Our results passed this module with very low adapter content **(below 0.8%)** across all positions, indicating minimal adapter contamination. ![](./assets/quality_res_byROA/Adapter%20Content1.png) |  |

## Trimming and Filtering

Based on the initial quality assessment, reads were trimmed to remove low-quality bases and sequencing adapters, ensuring that only high-quality sequences were retained for downstream analysis. For this the tool `Trimmomatic` was used.

```{=html}
<pre style="background-color:#dee2e6; color:#2c3143; border:none">
<b>Trimmomatic</b> flexible read trimming tool for Illumina NGS data
(Galaxy Version 0.39+galaxy2)
</pre>
```

We tested multiple trimming strategies for our data (see Table below). Based on a comparison of their performance and suitability, we selected the optimal approach for the final analysis (The final one).

```{r echo = FALSE}
totalSequences <- 1424257

PercentSequencesRemoved <- function(x){
  percentSequencesLeft <- ((x * 100) / totalSequences)
  round(100 - percentSequencesLeft, digits = 2)
}
```

| Trim number | Avg. quality required | Min. read length to keep | \% sequences removed |
|:----------------:|:----------------:|:----------------:|:----------------:|
| 1st | 20 | 70 | `r PercentSequencesRemoved(1172109)` |
| 2nd | 30 | 70 | `r PercentSequencesRemoved(754143)` |
| 3rd | 30 | 100 | `r PercentSequencesRemoved(639254)` |
| 4th | 30 | 50 | `r PercentSequencesRemoved(822515)` |
| 5th | 20 | 50 | `r PercentSequencesRemoved(1224621)` |

### Trimming

Based on our quality control results, we selected specific parameters for trimming with `Trimmomatic`. We kept the default values, applied CROP to 145 bases to remove positions beyond 145 that showed noise in the per base sequence content, used HEADCROP of 7 bases to eliminate low-quality bases from the read starts, and set MINLEN to 50 to discard short reads after trimming.

# Read Mapping

## Mapping with BWA

Filtered reads were aligned to the appropriate human reference genome using a short-read aligner.

```{=html}
<pre style="background-color:#dee2e6; color:#2c3143; border:none">
<b>Map with BWA-MEM</b> - map medium and long reads (> 100 bp) against reference genome
(Galaxy Version 0.7.19)
</pre>
```

**Tool Parameters**

| Input Parameter | Value |
|------------------------------------|------------------------------------|
| Will you select a reference genome from your history or use a built-in index? | cached |
| Using reference genome | hg38 |
| Single or Paired-end reads | paired |
| Select first set of reads |  |
| Select second set of reads |  |
| Enter mean, standard deviation, max, and min for insert lengths. | Not available. |
| Set read groups information? | do_not_set |
| Select analysis mode | illumina |
| BAM sorting mode | Sort by chromosomal coordinates |

### Expected coverage

Key alignment metrics such as mapping rate and coverage were evaluated.

A sequence's coverage or read depth is the average amount of reads of each region in a given genome. To calculate the coverage we can use the formula `C = LN/G`, where `C = coverage`, `L = read length`, `N = number of reads` and `G = captured region`. This results in an expected or estimated coverage, as many reads could not be distributed evenly.

```{r}
Coverage <- function(readLength, readAmount, capturedRegion){
  (readLength * readAmount) / capturedRegion
}
```

```{r}
# Our expected coverage on CardioPanel
#
# 50 min. & 138 max. sequence length
# 1206159 total sequences, times 2 strands
# 320000 bases for the CarioPanel 
Coverage(88, 1206159 * 2, 320000)

# "Max Illumina sequencer coverage on CardioPanel
#
# 300 max Illumina sequence length
# 25000000 max Illumina reads
# 320000 bases for the CardioPanel
Coverage(300, 25000000, 320000)
```

The resulting expected read depth is \~ 663. Which means spotted DNA variants should be of high confidence. However, the actual coverage of each region should be also checked after the following mapping steps.

### Marking Duplicate Mapped Reads

Before analyzing differences between the reference genome and our patient sample, duplicate mapped reads must be identified. Duplicates arise from PCR amplification bias (multiple copies of the same fragment) or optical artifacts during sequencing, and if unaddressed, can lead to false positive variant calls and inaccurate coverage estimates.

We used `MarkDuplicates` tool on the coordinate-sorted BAM files from the previous mapping step. The algorithm identifies duplicate pairs by comparing read coordinates, orientations, and insert sizes, then adds a duplicate flag to each identified duplicate read. Importantly, reads are flagged but not removed, preserving data integrity while allowing downstream tools to ignore these flagged reads during analysis.

```{=html}
<pre style="background-color:#dee2e6; color:#2c3143; border:none">
<b>MarkDuplicates</b> - examine aligned records in BAM datasets to locate duplicate molecules 
(Galaxy Version 3.1.1.0)
</pre>
```

**The output includes:**

A marked BAM file `.bam`: alignment data with duplicate flags

A BAM index file `.bai`: enables rapid random access for visualization

These files serve as input for the next step: visualizing the mapping data without the confounding effects of duplicates.

### Visualizing the Mapping Data

#### Integrative Genomics Viewer (IGV)

To visually inspect the mapped reads and identify potential variants, we used the **Integrative Genomics Viewer (IGV)**. This tool enabled visualization of read alignment, coverage depth, and nucleotide changes across target regions, using the BED file to navigate directly to genes of interest.

#### Reference Genome and Data Files

The reference genome used for visualization was **GRCh38/hg38** (Genome Reference Consortium Human Build 38), which provides a high-quality assembly of the human genome.

For this visualization step, we used two primary input files:

1.  **Marked BAM file** (`dataset.bam`): Contains the aligned reads with duplicate flags, enabling accurate visualization without PCR bias.

2.  **Target BED file** (`Reference-hg38.bed`): A interval file specifying all captured regions in the gene panel.

The BED file contains four columns specifying the chromosome, exon start and end positions, and gene name (e.g., PSEN2, LMNA), allowing us to navigate directly to regions of interest. This BED file served as a navigation guide, allowing us to rapidly zoom into specific genes of interest and examine their coverage and potential variants.

#### Variant Identification

Using the BED file to navigate, we examined two different genes of interest. Below are representative examples of variants identified in this analysis:

**Figure 1: PSEN2 Gene Region**

![](./assets/quality_res_byROA/mapping/variant_cropped.jpeg)

A variant was identified in the PSEN2 gene at the stop codon position. The reference sequence shows a stop codon (TGA), while the patient sample displays a T nucleotide (red) at this position, changing the codon to CGA, which encodes Arginine (ARG). This stop-loss variant would result in an extended protein product, potentially altering its normal function.

**Figure 2: LMNA Gene Region**

![](./assets/quality_res_byROA/mapping/3_cropped.jpeg)

Visualization of the LMNA gene showing a heterozygous variant. The aligned reads display both reference and alternative alleles (mixed colors at the variant position), with approximately equal representation. Heterozygous variants in LMNA are known to be associated with dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM).

# Mapping Quality Control

In this section, we assessed the mapping coverage for all panel genes to evaluate mapping performance. As observed in IGV, coverage levels varied significantly across regions, ranging from very high (300+) to areas with only a few reads present, which can impact variant detection reliability. Using **R** with libraries commonly used in genetic research, we calculated and reported coverage statistics for all panel genes to quantitatively assess these variations and identify undercovered regions.

## Loading the BED-data

The first step is to load the BED file containing the exon coordinates of our panel genes. The file is tab-separated and has four columns: chromosome, start, end, and gene name. We will read it into R, assign proper column names, and then examine the distribution of exons across chromosomes.

```{r}

bed_file <- "./Reference-hg38.bed"

exons <- read.table(bed_file, header = FALSE, sep = "\t", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

colnames(exons) <- c("chromosome", "start", "end", "gene")

# Count exons per chromosome
exon_counts <- table(exons$chromosome)

# Plot the number of exons per chromosome
barplot(exon_counts, 
        main = "Number of exons per chromosome",
        ylab = "Exon count",
        xlab = "Chromosome",
        las = 2,
        col = "#97cced",  
        border = "white" 
)
  

```

This barplot shows the number of exons located on each chromosome in our dataset. Chromosomes with higher exon counts typically contain more genes or longer genes with multiple exons. For example, chromosome 2 has the highest exon count (around 250-300). In contrast, chromosomes like chr18, chr20, and chrX have fewer exons, indicating they may contain fewer genes or genes with simpler structures.

## BED-visualization

In this section, we visualized the distribution of genes across different chromosomes using the BED data. First, we reduced the data to unique chromosome-gene combinations, then counted the number of genes per chromosome and presented the results in a bar plot. This visualization provides a clear overview of how genes are distributed across chromosomes, helping to identify which chromosomes carry the most genes in our panel.

```{r}
chromosome_gene <- subset(exons, select = c(chromosome, gene))

uni_gene <- unique(chromosome_gene)

gene_counts <- table(uni_gene$chromosome)

barplot(gene_counts, 
        main = "Number of gene per chromosome",
        ylab = "Number of genes",
        xlab = "Chromosome",
        las = 2,
         col = "#97cced",
        border = "white" 
    )
```

This plot shows the number of genes per chromosome, and it directly explains the previous exon distribution. Chromosome 2 has the highest gene count (7 genes), which is why it also had the highest exon count (250-300). Chromosomes with fewer genes consistently showed fewer exons, confirming that exon numbers reflect gene density across chromosomes.

## Bioconductor

Bioconductor is a repository containing over 1800 R packages specifically designed for analyzing high-throughput biological data, which we used throughout this assignment.

**Why Convert IRanges to GRanges?**

The IRanges object contains exon positions and lengths but lacks chromosome information, making it incomplete for genomic analysis. Converting to a GRanges object adds the chromosome context, creating a complete genomic coordinate system that properly locates each exon in the genome.

The BED file was first represented as an IRanges object since it contains simple positional data such as chromosome names and start/stop positions. These IRanges objects were then converted to GenomicRanges objects, which store genomic features (like exons) along with their chromosome coordinates and strand information.

```{r include=FALSE}
## Only needed when the package is missing
if (!require("BiocManager"))
    install.packages("BiocManager")

BiocManager::install("GenomicRanges")
```

```{r message=FALSE}
# This package contains the 'IRanges', 'GRanges' and 'GRangesList' classes we will use
library(GenomicRanges)
```

```{r}
# Split the data by gene, resulting in a list with named elements
bed_splitted <- split(exons, exons$gene)
my_list <- list()

for (gene in names(bed_splitted)[1:55]) {
  data <- bed_splitted[[gene]]
  ranges <- IRanges(start = data$start, end = data$end, names = data$gene)
  granges <- GRanges(seqnames = data$chromosome, ranges = ranges) 
  my_list[[gene]] <- granges
}

final_GRange_list <- GRangesList(my_list) 
head(final_GRange_list)
```

## Gene Lengths

After creating the GRanges objects, we calculated the length of each gene using the width and sum functions on the GRangesList. Since some genes are much longer than others, a standard barplot would be difficult to read. We used the `gap.barplot` function from the plotrix library, which allows us to create a barplot with a gap in the y-axis to accommodate extremely long genes while still showing variation among shorter genes.

```{r include=FALSE}
if (!require("plotrix"))
  install.packages("plotrix")
```

```{r message=FALSE}
library(plotrix)
```

```{r}
geneLengths <- sum(width(ranges(final_GRange_list)))
# Originally 123059
geneLengths["TTN"] <- 25000

barplot(geneLengths, axes = F, cex.names = 0.5, las = 2, ylim = c(0, 25000), main = "Gene Lengths", col = "#e3abeb")
axis(2, at = c(0, 5000, 10000, 15000, 20000, 25000), 
     labels = c("0", "5000", "10000", "15000", "20000", "123059"), las = 2)
axis.break(2, 20000, style = "gap", brw = 0.05)
```

## Loading the Mapped Reads

We used the output from the mapping step (the BAM file) to inspect the coverage of all mapped positions across our panel genes. The Rsamtools library provides the necessary functions to read and process this alignment data into GRanges objects for further analysis.

First, we used the *BamFile* function to create a reference to our BAM file and its index, which allowed us to access the alignment data efficiently without loading the entire file into memory. Then, to extract only our specific gene regions from the BED-data, we used the *ScanBamParam* function with GRanges objects to set the parameters for selection. Finally, we applied the *pileup* function to retrieve the coverage information for these regions, which returned the actual read counts at each position within our genes for downstream analysis. Here the pileup data for **TTN** gene.

```{r include=FALSE}
# Installing required library
if (!require("Rsamtools"))
  BiocManager::install("Rsamtools")
```

```{r message=FALSE}
# Loading the RSamtools library
library(Rsamtools)
```

```{r}
#Example pileup on TTN gene
bam_file <- BamFile(file="./MapReads.bam", index = "./MapReads.bai")

TTN_gene <- final_GRange_list[["TTN"]]

ScanParam_gene <-ScanBamParam(which = TTN_gene)

pileup_data <- pileup(file = bam_file, scanBamParam = ScanParam_gene)

head(pileup_data)
```

## Pileup Processing

Here, we will obtain the pileup data for all our genes and store it in a single object `pileup_list`. This will allow us to calculate the average coverage for each gene and identify positions with low coverage that may require further inspection.

```{r}
pileup_list <- list()

for (gene in names(final_GRange_list)) {
  data <- final_GRange_list[[gene]]
  ScanParam_gene <-ScanBamParam(which = data)
  pileup_data <- pileup(file = bam_file, scanBamParam = ScanParam_gene)
  pileup_list[[gene]] <- pileup_data
}
#Compare with TTN pileup above
head(pileup_list[["TTN"]])
```

This table shows the raw sequencing data for every position in our genes. Each row represents one nucleotide position, telling us which chromosome it's on, the exact location, which DNA strand the read came from, what base (A, T, G, or C) was detected, and how many times that base was seen. The last column just labels which gene the position belongs to. This data helps us see how well each region was covered during sequencing and spot any positions that might need a closer look.

## Coverage calculation and reporting

We calculated the per-position coverage for each gene using the *aggregate* function, which sums the count values for each unique position across all reads. For every gene, we then determined: the number of bases sequenced, the average coverage, the number of low-coverage positions (below 30), and the percentage of low-coverage positions. These four values were stored in a new data frame along with the gene name, and the final results were ordered by the percentage of low-coverage positions in descending order.

```{r}
per_position_coverage <- data.frame(Gene = character(),
                           NumBases = integer(),
                           AvgCoverage = numeric(),
                           LowCovPos = integer(),
                           LowCovPerc = numeric())

for (gene_name in names(pileup_list)) {
  
  gene_data <- pileup_list[[gene_name]]
  
  coverage <- aggregate(x = list(count = gene_data$count),
                       by = list(pos = gene_data$pos),
                       FUN = sum)
  
  num_bases <- nrow(coverage)
  avg_cov <- round(mean(coverage$count), digits = 1)
  low_cov_num <- sum(coverage$count < 30)
  low_cov_perc <- round((low_cov_num / num_bases) * 100, digits = 1)
  
  new_row <- list(Gene = gene_name,
                  NumBases = num_bases,
                  AvgCoverage = avg_cov,
                  LowCovPos = low_cov_num,
                  LowCovPerc = low_cov_perc)
  
  per_position_coverage <- rbind(per_position_coverage, new_row)
  
}

#All genes processed
print(per_position_coverage)
```

Coverage analysis across the 55 cardiomyopathy genes shows that the majority **(40 genes)** have excellent sequencing coverage with **0%** low coverage positions. However, several genes show concerning coverage gaps. JPH2 has the poorest coverage with **(30.7%)** of the gene falling below acceptable thresholds, followed by GATAD1 **(21.3%)**, TPM1 **(16.8%)**, and PRKAG2 **(16.3%)**. Other genes with significant coverage issues include DES **(14.7%)**, JUP **(11.2%)**, and MYBPC3 **(10.5%)**. These genes with \>10% low coverage warrant careful interpretation as potential variants in these poorly covered regions may be missed. In contrast, important large genes like TTN maintained excellent coverage throughout, increasing confidence in variant detection.

# Analysis of Variants

## Finding and Annotating Variants

Variant calling was performed to identify single nucleotide variants (SNVs) and small insertions/deletions (indels) from the aligned reads. We are interested in a single nucleotide variants (SNVs) only, thus we are using the default settings in the tool.

```{=html}
<pre style="background-color:#dee2e6; color:#2c3143; border:none">
<b>Call variants</b> with LoFreq
(Galaxy Version 2.1.5+galaxy3)
</pre>
```

**Tool Parameters**

|              Input Parameter               |        Value        |
|:------------------------------------------:|:-------------------:|
|         Input reads in BAM format          |                     |
| Choose the source for the reference genome |       cached        |
|              Reference genome              |        hg38         |
|            Call variants across            |       genome        |
|         Types of variants to call          |      Only SNVs      |
|         Variant calling parameters         |        false        |
|         Variant filter parameters          | set_lofreq_standard |
|                    sig                     |        0.01         |
|                    bonf                    |       dynamic       |
|                   others                   |       Empty.        |

## VCF File Fitlering

The result of the `LoFreq` tool is a single new file in your history in the vcf file format where each line describes a single variant. We have **1005** different variants.

```{r}
VCF_FILE <- read.delim("Call_variants.vcf", stringsAsFactors = FALSE , comment = "#")
head(VCF_FILE)
```

## VCF File Processing

To minimize false positive calls, variants were filtered using allele frequency. First we extract the allele frequency (AF) values from the VCF file. This AF data was subsequently incorporated as an additional column following the creation of GRanges objects.

```{r}
vcfInfo <- do.call(rbind, strsplit(VCF_FILE$INFO, ";"))

vcfInfo <- data.frame(vcfInfo)
names(vcfInfo) <- c("DP", "AF", "SB", "DP4")

alleleFreq <- as.numeric(gsub("AF=", x = vcfInfo$AF, ""))
```

Variants were subsequently filtered to retain only those with an allele frequency of ≥30%.

```{r}
vcfIRanges <- IRanges(start = VCF_FILE$POS, end = VCF_FILE$POS)

vcfGRanges <- GRanges(seqnames = VCF_FILE$CHROM, ranges = vcfIRanges )

mcols(vcfGRanges) <- DataFrame(AF = alleleFreq)

vcfGRangesFiltered <- vcfGRanges[vcfGRanges$AF >= 0.3]

vcfGRangesFiltered
```

To identify all variants falling within exonic regions, an overlap analysis was performed using the `findOverlaps` function. The resulting output contains two columns: `queryHits` and `subjectHits.` The `queryHits` column indicates the rows from the VCF data that lie within an exon, representing the variants of interest. The `subjectHits` column corresponds not to individual exons but to genes, meaning a `subjectHits` value of 1 refers to a hit within any exon of the first gene.

From the results, gene number 25 was observed to have 21 hits within its exonic regions.

```{r}
overlaps <- findOverlaps(vcfGRangesFiltered, final_GRange_list)
overlaps <- DataFrame(overlaps)
(overlaps)
```

After obtaining the row numbers of variants to retain, the filtered VCF file was reconstructed. This was achieved by reading the original VCF file with the `readLines` function. The header lines and variant rows were extracted separately, then recombined to generate the final filtered VCF file with `writeLines`.

```{r}
vcfLines <- readLines(con = file("./Call_variants.vcf"))

header_lines <- vcfLines[1:146]

variant_lines <- vcfLines[overlaps$queryHits + 147]

final_vcf <- c(header_lines, variant_lines)

writeLines(final_vcf, "filtered_variants.vcf")
```

### Variant Visualization

Two simple visualizations were created to explore the filtered variant dataset.

```{r}
hist(vcfGRangesFiltered$AF, breaks = 20, main = "Distribution of Allele Frequencies", ylim = c(0, 350),
     xlab = "Allele Frequency",
     ylab = "Number of Variants",
     col = "steelblue")
```

The two peaks in the allele frequency histogram correspond to the two possible zygosity states in a diploid genome:

-   **50%**: Heterozygous variants, where one copy carries the alternative allele and the other carries the reference allele

-   **100%**: Homozygous variants, where both copies carry the alternative allele

Next we can plot the number of variants per gene.

```{r include=FALSE}
# Installing required library
if (!require("ggplot2"))
  BiocManager::install("ggplot2")
```

```{r message=FALSE}
# Loading the ggplot2 library
library(ggplot2)
```

```{r}
variantFreq <- table(overlaps$subjectHits)

names(variantFreq) <- names(final_GRange_list)[as.integer(names(variantFreq))]

variantFreq <- data.frame(variantFreq)

names(variantFreq) <- c("gene_name", "variant_count")

ggplot(variantFreq, aes(x = gene_name, y = variant_count, fill = gene_name)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", show.legend = FALSE) +
  labs(title = "Number of Variants per Gene", x = "Genes", y = "Number of Variants") +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 20, by = 2)) +   # finer y‑axis breaks
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 20)) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, hjust = 1, vjust = 0.5))  # vertical labels
```

Looking at the distribution of variants across genes, **TTN** had the highest number with 19 variants, followed by **RYR2** with 11. **MYPN** and **DMD** each had 10 variants, while **MYH6** had 8. A few other genes like **DSP** (6) and **DES** (5) also showed moderate variant counts. The rest of the genes had smaller numbers, mostly between 1 and 3 variants.

What's interesting is that most of the genes with the highest variant counts are actually known to be involved in heart disease. So even though the variants are spread across many genes, the ones with the most hits tend to be those with known roles in cardiac function. This is not surprising, as our samples were obtained from patients with cardiomyopathy, so finding more variants in heart-disease-associated genes is expected.

# Variant Annotation

The filtered VCF file was uploaded to Galaxy for the subsequent annotation step to identify and characterize the genetic differences.

## SnpEff and SnpSift

Following variant calling with `LoFreq`, we performed three sequential annotation steps to add functional, clinical, and population-level information to our filtered VCF file.

**SnpEff – Functional Annotation**

We used `SnpEff` with the GRCh38.p14 genome reference to annotate our filtered VCF file. This tool adds functional predictions for each variant, including impact severity (HIGH, MODERATE, LOW, MODIFIER), gene names, transcript biotypes, and HGVS nomenclature. All annotation details are stored in the `ANN` field. The output consists of an annotated VCF file and a web-based summary report.

**SnpSift – dbSNP and ClinVar Annotation**

We ran `SnpSift` to add known variant identifiers and clinical significance data using the `dbSNP` database that includes `ClinVar` information. The `ID` column was populated with ClinVar identifiers, and the `INFO` field was expanded with clinical significance (CLNSIG), disease names (CLNDN), and review status (CLNREVSTAT) for known variants.

**SnpSift – dbNSFP Annotation**

We used `SnpSift` to annotate our VCF with the `dbNSFP` database, a comprehensive collection of over 300GB of integrated annotation sources. This step added population allele frequencies from gnomAD and ExAC, multiple in-silico prediction scores (including SIFT, PolyPhen, REVEL, CADD, and AlphaMissense), conservation metrics, and gene constraint information. The resulting file, `SnpVariants_Step3.vcf`, was used for subsequent filtering and analysis in Galaxy.

```{bash eval=FALSE}

java -jar /data/datasets/dbNSFP/snpEff/SnpSift.jar DbNsfp -db /data/datasets/dbNSFP/snpEff/data/dbNSFP5.3.1a_grch38.gz -n SnpVariants_Step2.vcf > SnpVariants_Step3.vcf

```

**Annotation Summary**

After completing the annotation workflow in Galaxy, we performed additional processing in R to extract and summarize the metadata from our annotated VCF file. The final output consolidates the key annotation data added during each step of the workflow. A brief summary of the added annotation sources and the types of values they provide is presented in the table below.

```{r include=FALSE}
if (!require(stringr))
  install.packages('stringr')
```

```{r message=FALSE}
library(stringr)
```

```{r}
#Read metadata description fields from final vcf file
snpVcf <- readLines("./SnpVariants_Step3.vcf")
snpVcf <- snpVcf[str_detect(snpVcf, "##INFO")]

#Remove identifier fields
snpVcf <- str_remove_all(snpVcf, "(##INFO=<ID=|Number=|Type=|Description=|\\\\|\"|>)")
snpVcf <- str_replace_all(snpVcf, ",\\s", "; ")

#Create table from resulting values
snpVcf <- read.table(text = snpVcf, sep = ",", fill = T, stringsAsFactors = FALSE, quote = "", col.names = c("ID", "Number", "Type", "Description"))

#Assign database
#Index 1 to 7 are from database Human Genome 38 (hg.38)
#Index 8 to 10 are from database GRCh38.p14, assignment step 1 (SnpEff)
#Index 11 to 31 are from database dbSnp_clinvar, assignment step 2 (SnpSift)
#Index 32 to 536 are from database dbNSFP, assignment step 3 (SnpSift)
snpVcf$Database <- c(replicate(7, "hg.38"), replicate(3, "GRCh38.p14"), replicate(21, "dbSnp_clinvar"), replicate(505, "dbNSFP5.3.1a"))
```

The file doesn't include explicit descriptions of the NSFP database fields. However, we can download the (documentation file)[<https://drive.google.com/file/d/1lx26ftYpsQEi5tp1LzF7a4U2Ak8oYKXn/view>] and parse it too.

## Analyzing Variant Annotation

After annotating our VCF file with functional, clinical, and population-level data, we performed additional data preparation steps to convert the complex annotation fields into a workable format suitable for filtering and ranking in R.

```{r}

#Read text documentation file
nsfpDocs <- readLines("./dbNSFP5.3.1a.readme.txt")
#Vector of IDs to compare against the many entries in the file
nsfpIDs <- snpVcf$ID[32:536]
nsfpIDs <- str_remove_all(nsfpIDs, " ")
nsfpIDs <- paste0(nsfpIDs, ":")

#Look up and add descriptions in correct order
#IMPORTANT: File has been edited with an IDE in order to simplify this R code.
nsfpDocsLines <- c()
for (id in nsfpIDs) {
  newLine <- nsfpDocs[str_detect(nsfpDocs, id)]
  if (length(newLine) > 1) {
    nsfpDocsLines <- c(nsfpDocsLines, newLine[1])
    next
  }
  if (identical(newLine, character(0))) {
    nsfpDocsLines <- c(nsfpDocsLines, "")
    next
  }
  nsfpDocsLines <- c(nsfpDocsLines, newLine)
}

#Remove unnecessary strings
nsfpDocsLines <- str_remove_all(nsfpDocsLines, "(.+:\\s|\\\t|\\\\|\")")

#Assign new descriptions to corresponding entries
snpVcf$Description[32:536] <- nsfpDocsLines
```

### Data Preparation

We used the `SnpSift` Extract Fields tool in Galaxy to extract specific annotation fields from the annotated VCF file into a tabular format. The final file includes the following selected columns:

| Column | Reason for Inclusion |
|------------------------------------|------------------------------------|
| CHROM, POS, ID, REF, ALT, FILTER | Core variant identification and quality control |
| ANN[\*].EFFECT | Specific molecular consequence (e.g., missense, stop_gained) |
| ANN[\*].IMPACT | Severity ranking (HIGH, MODERATE, LOW, MODIFIER) |
| ANN[\*].GENE | Gene symbol for biological context |
| ANN[\*].FEATURE | Feature type (transcript, regulatory region) |
| ANN[\*].FEATUREID | Unique transcript identifier for cross-referencing |
| ANN[\*].BIOTYPE | Transcript classification (protein_coding, pseudogene) |
| CLNDN, CLNSIG, CLNVC | Clinical significance and disease associations from ClinVar |
| dbNSFP_REVEL_score | Ensemble meta-predictor for missense pathogenicity |
| dbNSFP_SIFT_pred, dbNSFP_SIFT_score | SIFT prediction and score for missense deleteriousness |
| dbNSFP_Polyphen2_HDIV_pred, dbNSFP_Polyphen2_HVAR_pred | Polyphen2 predictions (human diversity and human variation modes) |
| dbNSFP_MutationTaster_pred | Comprehensive disease-causing prediction |
| dbNSFP_CADD_phred | Combined Annotation Dependent Depletion (CADD) phred score for variant deleteriousness |
| dbNSFP_VEST4_score | Variant Effect Scoring Tool (VEST4) for missense pathogenicity |
| dbNSFP_ESM1b_pred | Evolutionary Scale Modeling (ESM1b) prediction for protein variant effects |
| dbNSFP_phyloP100way_vertebrate | Phylogenetic conservation score across 100 vertebrates |
| dbNSFP_GERP\_**NR, dbNSFP_GERP**\_RS | Genomic Evolutionary Rate Profiling (GERP) rejected substitutions and neutral rate scores |
| dbNSFP_fathmm_XF_coding_pred | Functional Analysis Through Hidden Markov Models (fathmm) coding variant prediction |
| dbNSFP_BayesDel_addAF_pred | Bayesian deleteriousness prediction incorporating allele frequency |
| dbNSFP_MetaSVM_pred, dbNSFP_MetaLR_pred | Ensemble SVM and logistic regression meta-predictors for missense impact |

### Finding Variants of Interest

First, variants were filtered to retain only `missense_variant` and `splice_region_variant`, as these are more likely to have functional impact. Then, redundant entries were removed by collapsing variants that represent the same genomic change but appear multiple times due to different annotations.

After collapsing, 10 unique variants remained. These were further evaluated using the ClinVar database. Two variants (in POTEE and POTEI) were excluded as they are not associated with dilated cardiomyopathy.

The final table therefore includes 8 variants relevant to the disease.

```{r include=FALSE}
if (!require(tidyverse))
  install.packages('tidyverse')
```

```{r message=FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
```

```{r}
snpFilteredTable <- read.table("./ProcessedVariants.tabular", sep = "", quote = "", fill = T, header = T)
snpFilteredVariants <- filter(snpFilteredTable, str_detect(snpFilteredTable$ANN....EFFECT, "(missense_variant|splice_region_variant)"))
snpFilteredVariantsCollapsed <- distinct(snpFilteredVariants, snpFilteredVariants$POS, .keep_all = T)


for (pos in snpFilteredVariantsCollapsed$POS) {
  p <- filter(snpFilteredVariants, str_detect(snpFilteredVariants$POS, as.character(pos)))
  snpFilteredVariantsCollapsed$ANN....FEATUREID[which(snpFilteredVariantsCollapsed$POS == pos)] <- paste(p$ANN....FEATUREID, collapse = "|")
}
snpFilteredVariantsCollapsed <- filter(snpFilteredVariantsCollapsed, snpFilteredVariantsCollapsed$ANN....GENE %in% names(final_GRange_list))
snpFilteredVariantsCollapsed <- arrange(snpFilteredVariantsCollapsed, desc(snpFilteredVariantsCollapsed$ANN....IMPACT))
```

# Variant Visualization

## LollipopPlot

A `lollipop` plot was used to visualize the distribution of selected variants, particularly in cases where multiple variants are located within the same gene. In this plot, the x-axis represents the genomic position of each variant, while the y-axis represents the allele frequency (AF) derived from the VCF file, scaled by a factor of 100 to improve readability due to the small magnitude of the original values.

```{r include=FALSE}
if (!require(trackViewer))
  BiocManager::install("trackViewer")
```

```{r message=FALSE}
library(trackViewer)
```

```{r}
#Store all variants in each gene of interest
variantsTTN <- filter(snpFilteredTable, str_detect(snpFilteredTable$ANN....GENE, "TTN"))
variantsTTN <- distinct(variantsTTN, variantsTTN$POS, .keep_all = T)

variantsMYH6 <- filter(snpFilteredTable, str_detect(snpFilteredTable$ANN....GENE, "MYH6"))
variantsMYH6 <- distinct(variantsMYH6, variantsMYH6$POS, .keep_all = T)

variantsDMD <- filter(snpFilteredTable, str_detect(snpFilteredTable$ANN....GENE, "DMD"))
variantsDMD <- distinct(variantsDMD, variantsDMD$POS, .keep_all = T)

variantsLDB3 <- filter(snpFilteredTable, str_detect(snpFilteredTable$ANN....GENE, "LDB3"))
variantsLDB3 <- distinct(variantsLDB3, variantsLDB3$POS, .keep_all = T)
```

We can map the allele frequency from our genomic ranges object onto each gene's data frame. This is used for plotting purposes later, as the other values from dbNSFP seem incomplete in our tables.

```{r}
#Assign allele frequency to stored gene of interest variants
dfGranges <- GRanges(seqnames = variantsTTN$CHROM, ranges = variantsTTN$POS)
dfOverlaps <- DataFrame(findOverlaps(dfGranges, vcfGRanges))
variantsTTN$AF <- vcfGRanges[dfOverlaps$subjectHits]$AF

dfGranges <- GRanges(seqnames = variantsMYH6$CHROM, ranges = variantsMYH6$POS)
dfOverlaps <- DataFrame(findOverlaps(dfGranges, vcfGRanges))
variantsMYH6$AF <- vcfGRanges[dfOverlaps$subjectHits]$AF

dfGranges <- GRanges(seqnames = variantsDMD$CHROM, ranges = variantsDMD$POS)
dfOverlaps <- DataFrame(findOverlaps(dfGranges, vcfGRanges))
variantsDMD$AF <- vcfGRanges[dfOverlaps$subjectHits]$AF

dfGranges <- GRanges(seqnames = variantsLDB3$CHROM, ranges = variantsLDB3$POS)
dfOverlaps <- DataFrame(findOverlaps(dfGranges, vcfGRanges))
variantsLDB3$AF <- vcfGRanges[dfOverlaps$subjectHits]$AF
```

A custom R function, `plot_gene_lollipop`, was developed to generate lollipop plots for multiple genes. The function takes three inputs: the gene name, a variants data frame specific to that gene (prepared in a previous step), and a list of the original genomic features stored as GRanges objects.

Within the function, the variant data are converted into a GRanges object, where each variant is represented with its genomic position, allele frequency (AF), ID, effect, and impact. The corresponding gene features are retrieved from the provided features list and formatted for visualization.

Several visual attributes were then customized to encode biological meaning:

| Attribute | Description |
|------------------------------------|------------------------------------|
| **Score (y-axis)** | The allele frequency (AF) was used as the score after scaling it by 100 to improve readability. |
| **Color** | *missense_variant* variants were colored **red**, while *splice_region_variant* variants were colored **blue** to distinguish variant types. |
| **Size** | Node size reflects variant impact: **MODERATE** impact variants appear larger, while **LOW** impact variants are smaller, ensuring clear visual distinction. |
| **Shape** | Shapes were assigned based on variant effect: *missense variants* as **diamonds** and *splice region variants* as **squares**. |
| **Transparency & Border** | A consistent transparency (alpha = 0.8) and neutral border color were applied to enhance visual clarity. |

```{r}
# Create a function for any gene
plot_gene_lollipop <- function(gene_name, variants_df, features_list) {
  
  sample.gr <- GRanges(seqnames = variants_df$CHROM, 
                ranges = variants_df$POS,
                AF = variants_df$AF,
                POS = variants_df$POS,
                ANN....EFFECT = variants_df$ANN....EFFECT,
                ANN....IMPACT = variants_df$ANN....IMPACT)
  
  features <- features_list[[gene_name]]
  
  #set height and color height 
  features$fill <- c( "#51C6E6")
  features$height <-c(0.02)
  
  #set color for each node according to effect
  sample.gr$color[grepl("missense_variant", sample.gr$ANN....EFFECT)] <- "red"
  sample.gr$color[grepl("splice_region_variant", sample.gr$ANN....EFFECT)] <- "blue"
  
  sample.gr$alpha <- 0.8
  
  # set a score for each node 
  sample.gr$score <- sample.gr$AF * 100
  
  #sample.gr$node.label <- paste0(round(sample.gr$AF * 100, 1), "%")
  
  # Set label position
  #sample.gr$label.parameter.pos <- 3  
  
  # set a labels for each node according to ID 
  sample.gr <- setNames(sample.gr, sample.gr$POS)
  #sample.gr$label.parameter.rot <- 45 
  
  # set the size of node 
  # Ensure no node is too small to see
  #sample.gr$cex <- 1  # Default
  #sample.gr$cex[grepl("MODERATE", sample.gr$ANN....IMPACT)] <- 1.5
  #sample.gr$cex[grepl("LOW", sample.gr$ANN....IMPACT)] <- 0.8  # Minimum 0.8, not 0.5
  
  
  available.shapes <- c("circle", "square", "diamond", 
                        "triangle_point_up", "triangle_point_down")
  sample.gr$shape <- "circle"
  
  # Assign shapes based on impact
  sample.gr$shape[grepl("MODERATE", sample.gr$ANN....IMPACT)] <- "diamond"
  sample.gr$shape[grepl("LOW", sample.gr$ANN....IMPACT)] <- "square"  
  
  #sample.gr$shape <- sample(available.shapes, size = length(sample.gr), replace = TRUE)
  sample.gr$legend <- paste0("legend", as.numeric(factor(sample.gr$shape)))
  # set title for the graph 
  #grid.text(gene_name, x=.5, y=.98, just="top", gp=gpar(cex=1.5, fontface="bold"))
  
  # Plot
  lolliplot(sample.gr, features, ylab = "Allele Frequency (%)", type="circle", legend = list(labels = c("missense variant", "splice region variant", "intron variant"), fill = c("red", "blue", "white")), rescale = TRUE)
}

# Use for different genes
plot_gene_lollipop("TTN", variantsTTN, final_GRange_list)
plot_gene_lollipop("DMD", variantsDMD, final_GRange_list)
plot_gene_lollipop("MYH6", variantsMYH6, final_GRange_list)
plot_gene_lollipop("LDB3", variantsLDB3, final_GRange_list)
```

# Conclusion

This project presents a reproducible pipeline for variant discovery and prioritization in cardiomyopathy using NGS data. The workflow integrates quality control, filtering, annotation, and clinical interpretation. The identified variants provide a set of potential candidates, but further validation is required to confirm their pathogenicity.

Among the detected variants, `TTN` appears as the strongest candidate gene, while the remaining variants require further evidence before confirming pathogenicity. Validation was performed using ClinVar database annotation, supported by additional scoring systems from `dbNSFP`, `dbSNP`, and `ClinVar` annotations, which helped in assessing the clinical relevance of each variant.

This analysis has several limitations. It is based on a single sample, which limits generalizability. No functional validation was performed, so pathogenicity remains computationally inferred. Additionally, annotation scores were not consistently available across all variants, limiting direct comparison. Finally, some genes showed reduced sequencing coverage, which may lead to missed variants in low-coverage regions.
